title: Compressed Gas Storage
summary: Compressed gas cylinders must be stored, moved and placed with care to prevent tip-overs, leaks and fires. This talk covers OSHA's cylinder rules for welding and cutting work.
talking_points: Keep valve protection caps in place and secured when moving or storing cylinders.
Secure cylinders upright at all times, except for short periods while they are being hoisted or carried. Use a cylinder truck, chain or other steadying device so they cannot be knocked over.
Move cylinders by tilting and rolling them on their bottom edges. Do not drop them or let them strike each other violently.
Store oxygen cylinders at least 20 feet from fuel-gas cylinders or combustible materials, or behind a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet high with at least a one-half hour fire rating.

Inside buildings, store cylinders in a protected, well-ventilated, dry place at least 20 feet from highly combustible materials, and away from elevators, stairs and gangways. Never keep them in unventilated lockers or cupboards.
Keep cylinders far enough from welding or cutting that sparks, slag or flame cannot reach them. Do not strike an arc on a cylinder.
Do not take oxygen, acetylene or other fuel-gas cylinders into confined spaces.
Close the cylinder valve when work is done, when the cylinder is empty, and any time it is moved. Do not use a damaged or defective cylinder.
site_hazards_to_check: Cylinders standing loose with no chain, cart or other support
Oxygen stored near fuel gas, oil, grease or other combustibles
Cylinders in the path of sparks, hot slag or heat
Cylinders stored in closed lockers, stairwells or walkways
discussion_questions: How far apart are our oxygen and fuel-gas cylinders stored, and is that enough?
What do we use to keep cylinders from tipping while they are in use?
What do we do with a cylinder that is damaged or leaking?

attribution.notice: Adapted from 29 CFR 1926.350, Gas welding and cutting. Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by OSHA.
